analogy.p: Think of a dare between friends: the dared person often does something they know is wrong, not because they want to, but because they are terrified of being called a coward in front of the group. Lady Macbeth is the friend with the dare, and ‘Are you a man?’ is the taunt. The analogy captures how peer-style pressure about identity can override conscience. It breaks down because Macbeth is not a child, he already wants the crown, and the consequences are tragic and permanent, which makes his decision morally his own.

bullets: Three competing definitions of ‘a man’ run through the play: man as **daring and violent** (Lady Macbeth), man as **restrained by moral limits** (Macbeth in Act 1 Scene 7) and man as someone who **feels and protects** (Macduff, Malcolm, Siward).

The theme links directly to ambition (Macbeth acts to avoid seeming unmanly), to kingship (a true king should be a protector, a tyrant is a bully) and to appearance and reality (Lady Macbeth performs a hardness she cannot sustain).
Gender is also inverted: Lady Macbeth takes the ‘masculine’ role of decision-maker, and the witches have beards, so they blur the boundary between the sexes.
In an exam, always treat gender as a **question about power and identity**, not a list of what women and men do.

callouts.p: Shakespeare exposes ‘manliness’ as a dangerous performance: Macbeth proves his masculinity by killing, yet loses his humanity, while the play’s final values are loyalty, grief and protection.

core.h: What the theme is and why it matters
core.p: Gender in Macbeth is not simply about men and women. It is about **what a society demands of a man** and what happens when a man (or a woman) is pushed to prove it. In the first half of the play, ‘manhood’ is used as a weapon: Lady Macbeth turns it into a test of courage and Macbeth, desperate not to look weak, accepts the test. By the end, Shakespeare has shown that the cruelty they called manly destroys the very things that make a person human.

bullets: The imperative ‘unsex me here’ is a blunt command, and ‘unsex’ suggests that, to her, violence and ambition are masculine, while pity belongs to women. She is asking to be changed, which shows she believes she is not currently capable.

She asks for her ‘milk’ to be taken for ‘gall’. Milk (nourishment, motherhood) becomes gall (bitterness, poison): a perverted image of life turning into death. This anticipates the babies she later says she would kill in Scene 7.

‘Fill me from the crown to the toe’ followed by ‘direst cruelty’: the head-to-toe image shows she wants cruelty to take over her whole body, and the superlative ‘direst’ shows she cannot do half-measures.
She summons the spirits that ‘tend on mortal thoughts’, so her power is borrowed from the supernatural. A Jacobean audience would link a woman invoking spirits with witchcraft.
She also fears Macbeth’s nature: ‘Yet do I fear thy nature’. She sees him as ambitious but morally hesitant, and decides to ‘pour my spirits’ into his ear, so she takes the active, persuading role.

core.p: On reading Macbeth’s letter, Lady Macbeth immediately judges her husband’s character: she fears he is ‘too full o’ the milk of human kindness’. Notice that she treats kindness as a **flaw** and as something belonging to milk, the substance of mothers and babies. Her soliloquy then asks supernatural forces to remove her femininity so she can plan murder without pity.

bullets: Macbeth’s own definition, ‘I dare do all that may become a man’ followed by ‘Who dares do more is none’, is a moral definition. Note the caesura-like pause at the semicolon: he draws a clear **boundary** between being a man and being a monster.

Lady Macbeth redefines the boundary, so the argument is about who gets to define manhood. By the end of the scene he repeats her logic, praising her ‘undaunted mettle’ and saying she should ‘compose / Nothing but males’.
The scene closes with Macbeth’s couplet about hiding what the heart knows: his ‘false face’ is the first sign that his masculinity has become a performance.

callouts.p: ‘Afeard’ is an old-fashioned form of ‘afraid’. Comment on its sound and tone: she uses it as a taunt, and the blunt monosyllables make her argument sound simple and unanswerable. Then zoom out: the scene is structured as a question-and-answer duel which she wins.
callouts.t: AO2: zoom in on one word

core.p: In this pivotal scene Macbeth has decided against the murder (‘We will proceed no further in this business’). Lady Macbeth does not argue about right and wrong. She argues about **identity**, and that is why she wins. Examiners reward students who spot that the persuasion is emotional and personal, not logical.

head: Tactic
Example (Act 1 Sc 7)
Effect on Macbeth
rows: Mocks his resolve
‘Was the hope drunk / Wherein you dressed yourself?’
Suggests his ambition was weak and unreal; the clothing image links to ‘borrowed robes’ and to appearance and reality.
Questions courage
‘Art thou afeard’
‘afeard’ is a childish word; it suggests he is less than a man and a coward in love.
Defines manhood as action
‘When you durst do it, then you were a man’
Equates masculinity with daring; the conditional logic traps him: refuse, and he is not a man.
Raises the stakes
‘to be more than what you were’
Promises that murder will make him greater, which links manliness to status.
Shocking contrast
‘I have given suck’ and ‘dashed the brains out’
Her violent hypothetical shows a commitment he cannot match; the extreme image silences him.
Practical reassurance
‘screw your courage to the sticking-place’
Turns fear into a task; the plan makes the crime feel possible.

bullets: She also mocks him for being afraid of the sight of blood: ‘a heart so white’ is her phrase for his shame. White is the colour of cowardice, and she turns a moral weakness into a gendered insult.

In Act 3 Scene 2 the roles begin to swap. Macbeth now keeps his plans secret, calling her ‘dearest chuck’, a term that sounds affectionate and patronising: he is shutting her out of the decision to murder Banquo.

In Act 3 Scene 4 at the banquet Macbeth sees Banquo’s ghost. Lady Macbeth switches back to the old weapon: ‘Are you a man?’ and calls his fear ‘the very painting of your fear’. This time it fails, because he is fixed on his guilt, not his reputation.
Macbeth’s defiant reply, ‘What man dare, I dare’, shows him still using manhood as his measure. He then claims to be braver than any man who would face the ghost, so he is trapped in a performance.
By the end of Act 3 Macbeth says he is ‘in blood / Stepp’d in so far’. His masculinity has become a one-way journey in which retreat feels as hard as going forward.

callouts.p: She cannot kill Duncan because he resembles her father, and by Act 5 she cannot wash the blood away. A grade 9 answer argues that she **suppressed** her humanity and that the suppression eventually breaks her.
callouts.t: Do not say Lady Macbeth simply ‘has no feelings’

core.h: The testing of masculinity in Act 2 and Act 3
core.p: After Duncan’s murder the balance of power starts to shift. In Act 2 Scene 2 Lady Macbeth is the practical one, but she admits a limit: she could not kill Duncan because he looked like her father as he slept. Macbeth, in contrast, is horrified, so the partnership still depends on her calm. Her taunt ‘infirm of purpose’ shows she still uses gendered insults, and she takes the daggers back to the chamber herself.

bullets: The witches’ ambiguity mirrors Lady Macbeth’s request to be ‘unsexed’: both are women who step outside their expected roles, and in both cases the play connects that crossing of boundaries with evil and disorder.
Jacobean audiences believed in witchcraft. King James wrote Daemonologie (1597) and took the threat seriously, so the witches’ unnatural bodies would have felt dangerous and not comic.

The beards also prefigure the paradox of the prophecy: ‘none of woman born / Shall harm Macbeth’. The witches use gender as a trick: Macduff was ‘Untimely ripped’ from his mother’s womb, so he is technically not born in the usual way.
Macbeth’s last-act boast, that he cannot be harmed by any man born of woman, shows that his sense of invincibility is built on a loophole in the definition of manhood.

callouts.p: Macbeth’s fall comes from a man defined by an unusual birth. Shakespeare ironically ends the tyrant’s ‘manliness’ by a man whose mother’s body was violated.

core.p: Banquo meets the witches in Act 1 Scene 3 and cannot place them: ‘You should be women’ and yet their ‘beards forbid me’ to say so. They are ungendered, so they are unnatural and unclassifiable, which fits their role as agents of disorder. Their beards also make them symbols of female power taking a masculine form.

bullets: Macduff’s cry about his family (‘All my pretty ones?’) is a question, which shows him struggling to understand. The adjective ‘pretty’ makes the children small and vulnerable.
‘He has no children’ can refer to Macbeth, and it contrasts with Lady Macbeth’s earlier boast about what she would do to a baby. It shows how Macbeth’s violence ends the future.

In Act 4 Scene 2 Lady Macduff asks why her husband left, and she says he ‘wants the natural touch’. The wren image (the smallest bird fighting for her young against an owl) shows that **protection** is the natural instinct, so it indirectly condemns Macduff’s absence and Macbeth’s attack.

At the end Siward hears his son died fighting and is satisfied that he died ‘like a man’. Shakespeare balances this: Siward’s pride is conventional, but Malcolm replies that his death deserves more grief, and the play does not reduce soldiering to simple violence.
Malcolm’s test of Macduff in Act 4 Scene 3 (when he pretends to be lustful and greedy) proves that real masculinity is not just aggression. It is loyalty, responsibility and honesty.
core.h: Macduff, Malcolm and the alternative masculinity
core.p: In Act 4 the play brings in its answer. Lady Macduff and her children are murdered while Macduff is in England. When Ross brings him the news, Macduff is overwhelmed with grief. Malcolm urges him to ‘Dispute it like a man’, treating revenge as masculinity, but Macduff replies that he must ‘also feel it as a man’. The play endorses the second view: grief is part of being a man, not a threat to it.

head: Character
Definition of manhood they act on
How the play judges it
rows: Lady Macbeth
Daring, cruelty, readiness to kill
Collapses in Act 5 Scene 1; the ‘spot’ cannot be washed away.
Macbeth (Act 1)
Valour in battle, ‘brave Macbeth’, but moral limits
Praised in Scene 2 as ‘brave Macbeth’ for killing a rebel, so violence starts as heroic.
Macbeth (Act 5)
Defiance and isolation: ‘taste of fears’ forgotten
Becomes a tyrant who has lost all feeling; ‘Out, out, brief candle’.
Macduff
Protection and loyalty, plus the right to grieve
Rewarded: he kills Macbeth and restores order.
Banquo
Honour and caution; suspicious of ‘instruments of darkness’
Resists temptation, but murdered; his line continues.
Malcolm
Self-control and political skill
Becomes king; emerges as a calm, reflective leader.

bullets: The Great Chain of Being placed men above women in the household and God above the king. Lady Macbeth’s attempt to command her husband breaks the household order, just as regicide breaks the political order.

A powerful woman who persuades her husband to murder echoes Eve in the Bible: a woman who tempts a man to sin. Use this as a possible Jacobean reading, but also say a modern audience might sympathise with her as a woman who can only reach power through a man.

Because boy actors played Lady Macbeth, her speech about ‘unsex me’ would have been delivered by a male actor playing a woman rejecting womanhood, which adds an extra layer of irony. Mention this carefully, as a possibility.

Do not write ‘in those days women were treated badly’. Instead, link context to a specific moment, for example: a Jacobean audience, expecting wives to obey, would have been shocked by her commanding tone in 1.5.

callouts.p: Choose one precise contextual idea, name where it applies in the text, and use it to explain the writer’s purpose. For example: the unnatural reversal of gender roles mirrors the unnatural killing of a king, so Shakespeare presents both as threats to divine order.

core.h: Context for AO3: Jacobean views of gender and power
core.p: In early 17th-century England, society was **patriarchal**: men governed households and kingdoms, and women were expected to be obedient, chaste and silent. Women could not act on the public stage; boy actors played female roles. Macbeth was written in the reign of James I (crowned 1603), a king who wrote about kingship and witchcraft, so a ruler’s masculinity and legitimacy mattered to the audience.

bullets: **Traditional reading:** Lady Macbeth is a monstrous woman who destroys the natural order and is punished by madness and suicide, which supports the Jacobean idea that women who step outside their role bring ruin.

**Feminist reading:** she is an ambitious woman in a society that gives her no power except through her husband, so her cry ‘unsex me’ reveals the limits placed on women, and her collapse shows the cost of suppressing herself.
**Critique of masculinity:** Shakespeare shows that the pressure to look brave destroys men too. Macbeth does evil because he is afraid of seeming afraid.

**Counter-argument:** Lady Macbeth is not a victim, as she is the first to plan murder. Macbeth also has his own ambition before she speaks, since he is troubled by the prophecy in 1.3. A good answer says gender is the **method** of persuasion, not the entire cause.

callouts.p: Do not write that Lady Macbeth ‘made’ Macbeth do it. He freely chooses. Write that she **pressures** and **manipulates**, and that he is vulnerable because he already desires the crown.

core.p: Strong answers show that the text allows more than one reading. This is how you reach the higher bands for AO1: an exploratory argument rather than one fixed claim. Always back each reading with a quotation and a reason.

bullets: For an extract of 1.5 or 1.7: name the technique (imperative, rhetorical question, conditional, semantic field of birth and death) and say what it shows about the gender ideas of the time.
For the recalled-quotation part (b): choose three moments from different acts, such as 1.7, 3.4 and 4.3, to show development and contrast.
Build a ‘zoom’ in every paragraph: a word, a technique, then what Shakespeare is saying overall. End with a short context link if it genuinely fits.
Check your quotations are short (a few words) and embedded in your own sentence; paraphrase the rest.

callouts.p: Shakespeare presents masculinity as a dangerous performance: Macbeth’s need to prove himself leads him to destroy the loyalty, kinship and compassion that the play finally identifies as true manhood.
A social system in which men hold the main power in the family, society and government.

core.p: Edexcel’s Shakespeare question (40 marks including a short AO4 element) typically gives an extract and asks how a character or idea is presented, then asks you to link to elsewhere in the play. Both parts need quotation, analysis and context. For gender, plan for a conceptual thesis, not a character summary.

plan: Lady Macbeth redefines manhood as daring in 1.5 and 1.7
Macbeth’s own definition (restraint) and how it collapses
The inversion of the marriage and the failure of the taunt at the banquet (3.4)
Macduff’s ‘feel it as a man’ as the play’s alternative
Conclusion: Shakespeare’s purpose, linked to Jacobean views of order
essays.q: Explore how Shakespeare presents ideas about masculinity in Macbeth. (Part (b) style: refer to the extract from Act 1 Scene 7 and elsewhere in the play.)
essays.text:
Shakespeare turns masculinity into a weapon and then shows what it destroys. In Act 1 Scene 5 Lady Macbeth begins by fearing that her husband is too kind, calling his nature ‘the milk of human kindness’. The metaphor places compassion in the language of nursing, so she treats pity as feminine, and therefore as a defect in a would-be king. Her answer is the imperative ‘unsex me here’, which suggests that for her, ambition and cruelty are masculine properties that can be summoned as if by magic. A Jacobean audience, used to obedient wives and to boy actors in female roles, would hear a woman invoking spirits to cross a boundary, and might well link the speech with witchcraft.

The turning point comes in Act 1 Scene 7, where Macbeth has resolved not to kill Duncan. Shakespeare structures the scene as a duel in which Lady Macbeth never discusses morality. She attacks his identity: ‘Art thou afeard’ is a taunt whose childish register reduces him to a coward, and ‘When you durst do it, then you were a man’ gives him an impossible logic, since refusing now means he is not a man. Macbeth’s own definition, ‘Who dares do more is none’, is a moral and balanced epigram, so his surrender is all the more tragic: he knows the limit and crosses it because he fears being thought less than a man. Her shocking hypothetical, ‘I have given suck’, twists maternal tenderness into violence and silences him, and the scene ends with his admiration for her ‘undaunted mettle’.

Yet the play does not allow this definition of manhood to succeed. By Act 3 the marriage is inverted. Macbeth now calls his wife ‘dearest chuck’, a phrase that sounds affectionate but patronising, because he is keeping the plan to kill Banquo secret. At the banquet in 3.4, Lady Macbeth repeats her old weapon, ‘Are you a man?’, but it no longer works. The structure shows a reversal: the person who once controlled the argument now improvises while he is lost in guilt. We could interpret this as Shakespeare’s criticism of performative manhood, since both characters are trapped by the roles they chose. The later sleepwalking scene, with its washing of imaginary blood, suggests that her suppressed femininity and conscience cannot be unsexed forever.

In contrast, Macduff, in Act 4 Scene 3, offers an alternative. When Malcolm advises him to ‘Dispute it like a man’, Macduff answers that he must ‘also feel it as a man’. The modal verb ‘must’ gives grief the force of duty. Shakespeare places this exchange after the murder of Lady Macduff and her children, so the audience sees the true cost of Macbeth’s violence and learns what the play values. Even Siward’s calm acceptance of his son’s death is balanced by Malcolm’s assertion that the death deserves more grief, which shows that the play is wary of reducing manhood to battle. For an audience in the reign of James I, who saw kingship as a sacred duty to protect, a king who kills women and children is not a man but a tyrant.

Finally, Macbeth’s last scenes show the emptiness of his performance. He has ‘almost forgot the taste of fears’, and the adverb ‘almost’ hints that something human remains. His life becomes ‘a walking shadow’, a metaphor that strips him of substance. Shakespeare’s purpose is therefore not to condemn women who seek power, but to warn that when manhood is defined as the ability to kill, the result is isolation and a loss of self. The true masculine virtues of the play are loyalty, grief and protection, and they belong to the men who restore order.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare presents masculinity as a dangerous performance: the pressure to prove manhood drives Macbeth to destroy the compassion and loyalty that the play ultimately defines as true strength.
why: AO1: a conceptual thesis (masculinity as performance) is sustained across five paragraphs rather than describing characters in turn.
AO2: zooms into single words (‘afeard’, ‘dearest chuck’, ‘must’, ‘almost’), comments on imperative, modal verb, epigram and structure of the scene as a duel.
AO3: context is woven into the argument (boy actors, witchcraft belief, expectations of obedient wives, kingship as protection) rather than bolted on.
Offers alternative interpretations (criticism of performative manhood, wariness over Siward) and evaluates Shakespeare’s purpose in the conclusion.
AO4: varied sentence structures and precise vocabulary (inverted, patronising, performative); quotations are short and embedded.

model: Thesis: her power is real but borrowed and unstable, rooted in manipulation of Macbeth’s masculinity
Extract: ‘When you durst do it, then you were a man’ and ‘Art thou afeard’ show manipulation of his identity
Structure: duel-like exchange; Macbeth’s resistance gives way
Link: ‘unsex me here’ (1.5), ‘infirm of purpose’ (2.2), role reversal at 3.4
Counter: her sleepwalking in 5.1 shows the power cost
Context: Jacobean views on wifely obedience and women who tempt men; the Eve reading
Evaluate Shakespeare’s purpose: critique of manhood, not simply a condemnation of women
exam.q: Starting with this speech (Act 1 Scene 7, Lady Macbeth persuading Macbeth), explain how far you think Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a powerful woman. Refer to the extract and the play as a whole. (40 marks)
exam.tip: This is an AO1/AO2/AO3 question plus AO4. The mark scheme rewards a sustained conceptual line: explore ‘how far’ with both sides. Check marks on your paper.

model: Imperatives: ‘unsex me here’ shows command and urgency
Semantic field of nursing twisted: ‘milk’ becomes ‘gall’
Hyperbole: ‘top-full / Of direst cruelty’ shows total transformation
Supernatural invocation links to witchcraft
Soliloquy lets us see her private intent
AO3: ideas about women’s roles and witchcraft in the Jacobean period

exam.tip: Pick 3 or 4 precise quotations and zoom in on single words. Do not narrate.

mistakes.r: She manipulates through his fear of seeming unmanly, but Macbeth chooses; she also breaks down in 5.1, so Shakespeare shows the cost of suppressed conscience.
mistakes.w: Lady Macbeth is just an evil woman who controls Macbeth.

mistakes.r: Begin with an argument (manhood becomes a weapon) and use the scene as evidence; keep the plot to a minimum.
mistakes.w: Narrating what happens in 1.7 line by line.

mistakes.r: Link a specific idea (the expectation of obedient, silent wives) to a specific moment and to Shakespeare’s purpose.
mistakes.w: Writing ‘women were weak in those days’ as context.

mistakes.r: Name the technique, quote the word, then explain what it shows about her desperation and her view of femininity.
mistakes.w: Feature-spotting: ‘this is an imperative’ with no effect.

mistakes.r: Embed two to four words, such as ‘unsex me here’, and analyse each in turn.
mistakes.w: Quoting four lines of the soliloquy.

mistakes.r: Use the witches (beards), Macduff (‘feel it as a man’) and the ‘woman born’ prophecy to show the theme across the play.
mistakes.w: Ignoring the witches and Macduff, as if gender were only about the Macbeths.

mistakes.r: Argue that he is torn between ambition and conscience, and that manhood is the pressure point she uses.
mistakes.w: Saying Macbeth is weak because he listens to his wife.

quotes.a: The blunt imperative shows Lady Macbeth demanding that spirits remove her femininity, which she equates with pity. The verb ‘unsex’ implies that gender is something that can be stripped, and suggests she believes cruelty is masculine. A modern reading sees a woman who cannot access power as herself.
quotes.c: Jacobean audiences linked women who invoke spirits with witchcraft and disorder.

quotes.a: She names Macbeth’s compassion as ‘milk’, a feminine and nurturing image, which she regards as a weakness. The metaphor also introduces the milk and gall imagery that later turns motherhood into violence, so her language is gendered from the start.
quotes.c: Kindness is treated as unfit for a man who wants a crown.

quotes.a: Milk, which feeds babies, becomes gall, a bitter poison. This perversion of nourishment shows Lady Macbeth willing to corrupt her own body. It foreshadows the violent baby image in 1.7 and the murder of Lady Macduff’s children.
quotes.c: Motherhood was the central role expected of Jacobean wives.

quotes.a: The conditional structure turns manhood into proof: only by killing can he be a man. The archaic ‘durst’ suggests daring and challenge, like a schoolyard taunt, and the logic leaves Macbeth no honourable way to refuse.
quotes.c: Honour and courage were linked to masculinity in Jacobean culture.

quotes.a: Macbeth’s definition sets a moral limit to manhood; one who goes beyond it is not just less a man but nothing, which hints at the loss of humanity. The paradox shows he understands the cost, so his later choice is knowing and tragic.
quotes.c: Links to the idea that regicide breaks natural and divine order.
quotes.q: Who dares do more is none

quotes.a: Lady Macbeth uses maternal experience as a weapon, contrasting a mother’s tenderness with her claim she would kill her baby. The jarring juxtaposition shocks Macbeth into submission. It reveals how far she believes ambition and violence should override natural feeling.
quotes.c: Offends the Jacobean ideal of a nurturing mother.

quotes.a: The blunt rhetorical question repeats her 1.7 weapon, but now it fails: Macbeth is looking at the ghost. The question marks the point at which her control over him ends, and its short syntax sounds panicked, not commanding.
quotes.c: A king’s weakness shown before nobles threatens legitimacy.

quotes.a: The affectionate endearment seems tender but is condescending: Macbeth is excluding his wife from the plan to kill Banquo. Both tone and secrecy show the shift in the marriage, as he becomes the dominant partner in evil and she is reduced to a bystander.
quotes.c: A king taking control; the queen becomes subordinate.

quotes.a: In answer to Malcolm’s advice to ‘Dispute it like a man’, Macduff insists that grief is part of manhood. The modal ‘must’ stresses duty, and the line gives the play’s moral answer: compassion is not weakness. This directly contrasts Macbeth’s numbness.
quotes.c: Gives a model of masculinity suited to a legitimate ruler.

quotes.a: Macbeth reports that he has almost forgotten what fear tastes like. The sensory image shows how numbness has replaced conscience, and the contrast with his earlier horror at the dagger shows the damage caused by repeated killing. The word ‘almost’ suggests he is not entirely dead inside.
quotes.c: Shows the cost of ambition for a would-be great man.
quotes.ref: Act 5 Sc 5, early in the scene

quotes.a: The apparition’s promise makes Macbeth believe he is invincible, but the phrasing is equivocal. The emphasis on birth links the play’s gender themes to its ironies: the man who kills Macbeth is defined by an unnatural birth.
quotes.c: Equivocation was a topical fear after the Gunpowder Plot.

summary: Macbeth presents masculinity as something performed, tested and manipulated: characters define being a ‘man’ as violence, restraint or compassion, and the play judges those definitions. You must be able to trace this across the play, link it to Jacobean ideas about gender and kingship, and analyse the language and structure that carry it.

terms.d: A society in which men hold power over women in politics, law and the family.
A reversal of the expected order, for example Lady Macbeth taking the commanding role in the marriage.
A command form of a verb, such as ‘unsex me’, which shows demand and urgency.
A speech in which a character speaks their thoughts aloud, alone on stage, revealing true intentions.
A group of words linked by a shared meaning; e.g. milk, gall, babe, suck form a field of motherhood twisted into violence.
Excessive pride or self-confidence, which in tragedy leads to a downfall.
A character who contrasts with another to highlight qualities; Macduff is a foil for Macbeth.
The loss of masculine identity or power, or making a man feel less manly.
Using language that has two meanings in order to mislead; the witches’ prophecies about ‘woman born’ are an example.
